The Beginnning of the Runciman Mission.
When W went to London from Oban for his LMS
meeting _ Halifax sent for him + apparently
suggested an ill digested scheme that R
shd go to Prague just to be there + give if
possible sound advice to the 2 Parties.
W also consulted H Smythe when he returned
+ we all agreed that it was an impossible
task to go just like that, looked like superseding
the Ambassador + perhaps doing no good at all.
However a subsequent letter put the proposition
much more fully really involving a quite different
suggestion. So W replied that he would come +
see him +would Tuesday 5th do. So this was
agreed + we cut our yachting short by only
a day or two + returned to London on morning
of 5th.
After talks +interviews W decided he cd not
refuse provided he was described as a Mediator
not Arbitrator +provided both sides Czechs +
Sudeten Germans welcomed him.
But it was all to be kept very secret till
this approval from both sides was obtained.

Monday 11 - Monday 18
All this seemed to take a long time. It naturally
filled our minds very much. W at first
doubtful if he wd. be accepted + very doubtful
if there was any real chance of success.
He went about his usual Bank work
on the Tuesday + Wed: I have no records of
what we did. I spent some time ordering
more thin clothes because it was clear that
once it was fixed up we should have to start
at once. On the Sunday we went down to
Puddephats I had been before + found Kit
very well + very happy about her prospects.
She said that Oliver had been quite different
that last fortnight, he had apparently almost
given up all hope of ever having a child
in spite of Kitty's determined optimism.
On Monday I had my Marie Curie meeting. Funds
not too good. The Committee are always very
pleasant to me but I am concerned about
money raising. I haven't yet succeeded in
getting a really good committee together for Appeal
work.
19 Tuesday
I went to a Committee meeting to discuss the possibility
of a Gov: site now being vacated from positive
but impossible building. If however we could

Monday 18 - Monday 25th.
get it rent free as did the Scientific Researchers
who are now vacating it, it wd be worth while
trying to raise the money.
Wed 20th I felt I could not delay going to Doxford
So much to be done in rearranging furniture
now being stacked in all the rooms. Ruth
came with me. And we had some
strenuous days planning different rooms
+ having usual disappointments over dilatory
plumbers etc. However all agreed that cutting
off the servants wing was a good idea.
And taking away the staircase in visitors
corridor has added a substantial piece to
West East spare room making a really good
room of it. I could not complete everything
but stayed an extra day on W's assurance
that we wouldnt have to start for Prague
that week! We had some exciting conversations
through the telephone. There was a little
delay over the Sudeten's acceptance +
indeed the news leaked out from Prague
a day or two too soon. The News Chronicle
got it! It was apparently in London papers
on the Sat: with W's name suggested.
It began to be clear that it was really coming off

Monday 25th
I longed to be back in London with W at this
exciting time.
I was sorry to miss Chamberlain announcing
it in H of C. His references to W all that any
friend cd desire spoke of his fearlessness
integrity, liberal outlook etc. + said that those
who had worked most closely with him had learnt
best to appreciate his quality. And this we hear
was all very well received.
Wednesday +Thursday very busy days for me
clothes etc. I went to that dull assembly H of L
for first time as a Peeress to hear Halifax make
his announcement but after waiting hours learnt
through Lady Elibank who gave me tea who got
a note from her husband that H wd not come on
till 7.15 so as Leslie was coming to see us
I went back + didn't return. H explained
that W wd have to be quite independent of Gov:
acting on no instructions, responsible to no one +
he added that W had said "I quite understand, you
are setting me adrift in a small boat in
mid Atlantic" to which H replied "That is
exactly the position." which caused amusement.
Ernest Brown at Cowes said to me of course
W wouldn't say 'a small boat' he wd say "dinghey"
only H feared their Lordships 'wouldn't understand.'
Halifax announced Monday as the day of departure but we got it
[ ] made Tuesday.

Monday Aug. 1
It was very exciting this week to see the press
comments. Almost overwhelming the chorus of praise
at the choice of W. + confidence in his being
the "only man" who had a chance of success. W was
amazed, but I confess I expected it! though
perhaps not from some of the usually sneering
or hostile papers. The Manchester Guardian + News
Chronicle not too nice, trying to find something
to crab all the time, but Daily Mail Ev: Standard
etc very friendly.
W went down to Cowes on Thursday Wed:. I paid a
farewell visit to Kitty + followed on Thursday
afternoon. We had on board the Louis Griegs
he is a real charmer + Frank Curzon, a tall
thin upright man of 72, a great admirer of
his brother, a real nice Tory type but real Tory!
Ruth + George + Philip. It was all very pleasant.
This year we do seem to have had exceptionally
appreciative guests! We had a sail on
Saturday + went on the "Laura" but
there was not a great crowd. We saw the
Camroses. W had a long talk with him said he
wanted to be very helpful. W + Mr C. went on
Duke of Sutherland's yacht which they greatly
admired thought her perfectly fitted up.
I left on Sunday evening - The Vincent Baddeleys

Cowes
came on board to tea on Sunday. W came up
early on the Monday. I needed him to
sort out my yachts things which had
been on board since April.
Monday Bank Holiday Aug: 1
Busy day packing + writing final letters.
A lot of people have written very nice letters.
Mackenzie King PM of Canada sent a telegram,
Archbip a letter + old Mr Lansbury. Of ex colleagues
Hailsham Jem Stanhope Malcolm Macdonald +
of course the P. M + Halifax sent farewell notes.
The P. M had expressed th his thanks to W for under-
taking this difficult job, when he passed him
at the Garden Party, to which I cd not go as it clashed
with Marie Curie General meeting. Halifax has
been very sympathetic + nice all through +
W began after some talks to get a little
behind Cadogans silent or shy demeanour.
On Monday Oliver telephoned to say Kitty had gone to bed
not very sure what might happen. This came as
a great blow + I don't think we either of us slept
that night thinking of the terrible disappointment

to those poor children. We had however no rush
on Monday, and we had the morning of Tuesday
as well which gave a nice unhurried feeling.
W had got the team he wanted, not large. Mr
Stopford who had been sec to John Simon at
Indian Commission, Mr Gwatkin of F. O
lent for the time. Economics side. W had worked
with him + had marked him as a good man
Then he has Miss Miller + a typist lent also
from F. O. Geoffrey Peto offered to come + is
very welcome.
Monday night. I suddenly decided I must run
down to see Kitty so I was up by 8 o'clock + got
to Puddy 10 past nine to find K getting on well
"every hope" + a very nice bright young nurse,
who however obviously didn't want me to
stay lest Kitty shd talk too much so I only
stopped a few minutes but had the satisfaction
of knowing that all went was going on well + she had the
right kind of lend-a-hand nurse so essential in a
small house.

Mission to Prague
We left Victoria at 2 o'clock. The staff had
left the day before, a 4 hours journey by air!
We had abt 12 photographers on the door
step as we left 8 B. S. a score or so at
Victoria station. All very good humoured +
exhorting us to smile. 'Billy' Brown came to see
us off, full of advice to the last moment + no
doubt very excellent advice, but I wonder if he
isn't getting a little bit too much of a 'know all'!
He says he sees no holiday in prospect with
India + U S A Trade agreements at critical
stages, and he certainly needs a holiday. Halifax
sent some one +there were one or two others.
Geoffrey Peto joined us at station, very pleasant
to have him on the train, he looked after tickets
payments etc. + saved us all p[---] trouble.
Geoffrey Dawson came to see W on Monday
night, anxious to be very helpful.
A pleasant crossing, but I tried to sleep in
the cabin being most uncomfortably sleepy.
The Commissioner of Police consul + another
met us on the boat, and as we waited for the
crowd to get off, ("Il faut être le premier ou le
dernier" said the Commissioner very justly, he was
a jolly little man with a shrewd face.) several

people recognising W wished him well. In Cowes
on Sunday he was prayed for in Church!
The berths were quite comfy, it was just rather
hot especially the next morning otherwise
the journey was all right. Mr Peto tackled
I think 2 enterprising journalists. One a very
nice young man who finally was allowed to
come + speak to us not on politics he had
journeyed all the way to the frontier from Prague
+ didn't want to waste all this effort! At
Pilsener the Station Master came to tell us we
were to go to a different hotel to what we
expected + that over 100 journalists were
coming to the Alcron Hotel at 6 o'clock + that
he was to see Ministers next morning.
My German was fortunately equal to under-
standing this message. Earlier on at the
frontier a card was handed in from the
RC. Archbishop of Eger who said the police wd
not let him come on to the train but he
wished to welcome us + to tell as that
"wie am Sonntag in England" he would the next
day have a Mass for the Mission. So
perhaps our little RYS parson at Cowes wasn't
the only one to offer prayer in Church last Sunday.
People clearly are much moved by this

effort. It makes it all very responsible for W.
We reached Prague just before 3. Quite a good
little crowd at the station + representatives of
the chief ministers of state. Mr Newton our
Minister presented the 1st who presented the
rest. All smiles and pleasantries. Lots of
photographers from all angles, one from
a motor ahead of us cinematographed us
through our car windows! A great many
waves + hats off on the short drive + then
on arriving at the Hotel we went straight
to our rooms. The offices + bedrooms all in
one floor, quite a good suite. They seem
a nice team. There was a jolly photograph of
Miss Miller on her arrival with Mr Stopford
at the aerodrome. She is in fine spirits de-
lighted to be here + determined to justify her inclusion.
We had all 3 hours to cool down or try to +
bath +change before the meeting of
journalists. They were numberless, many
of them photographers. W practically read his
speech which I regretted, it always I think
diminishes the strength of his personality in speaking
but I think he^ just said the right thing. That the
post was not of his seeking but he had been assured
that he would be welcomed by both sides. That his

Wednesday 3 August.
long 40 years experience of public affairs had taught
him that no lasting agreement settlement can only be based
on mutual consent - that he was friend of all
+ enemy of none -That with good will only
a solution cd be found but with good will
it + he exhorted the press to use their
great influence in doing all possible to promote
this good will
Then he told them not to ask any questions
this time because he could certainly not
answer them.
Then he went down amongst them + talked to
several.
Apparently the staff are quite pleased with
the start.
In the evening we had a very pleasant
cool time dining on the large terrace of
the Legation looking down on the town, the
big domed church + the old 2 spired Church
flood lit, giving interest to the view. We
were just ourselves + Geoffrey + the Minister +
Mr Troutbeck of the Legation. The Minister is a
brother of Douglas Ettersley - not^very clever I shd say
but very pleasant + of nice disposition. His
house is built on side of a hill + is very high

innumerable steps even to the dining room
+ terrace + the garden is higher still + bedroom
on 5th floor: But the air was delicious not
nearly so stuffy as at Prague.
We didn't sleep very well it was hot + then
early morning was cold.
Wednesday. 3
The press quite satisfactory. One a
Sudeten paper unkindly describes W as
an ^ distinguished looking old gentleman dressed in Pre War fashion
clothing, but typical of the true English
aristocrat! And the suit was bought for
Ottawa only 6 years ago!
The Czech press perhaps a little more definitely
friendly then the Sudetens, ^ who, I suppose ^ are afraid to
commit themselves, they describe themselves
as friendlily sceptical but quite ready
to wait + see.
I find I can read a good deal without a
dictionary except when I want to be sure of
the exact meaning.
I have had 2 or 3 letters from well wishers
+ alas already 3 begging letters from apparently
educated Germans. I have the offer of a
dog + a present of little prints of old Prague

from some one who 40 years ago had a happy
time in England.
The hotel is most attentive almost painfully
so, the bows are so deep!
W + I have moved our quarters to the floor
above where we have 3 rooms communicating
+ where we hope we may find the air
a little fresher.
Certainly Prague is hot + stuffy, but there
seem to be lots of nice places where one can
get into higher air + dine in the evenings.
Thursday 4.
This morning W + all the 3 went in formal
attire to call on the Foreign Minister, + then
W went alone to the Prime Minister Mr Hodza
+ to the President Mr Benes, far the cleverest
he said.
All seem eager to make use of him + ready
to give all possible information. I think he
came back pleased with his calls.
None cd give any information as to Berlin
which is a little uncomfortable - they can get
no information.
Now nearly 7 o 'clock I suppose W is still
interviewing the Sudeten leader who was to come
at 5!

When I went down I found W writing a letter to
Edward Halifax sending him his statement
to Journalists + not drawing a rosy picture but
saying everyone was accessible.
The Sudetens he found much stiffer, a Committee
of them came without Henlein whom I am inclined
to think is still in Germany. However he
succeeded in thawing them. He said they were
as bad as de Valera men, would talk of what
happened 1000 years ago. W told them he could
only negotiate on the present + future. They
arranged to come back at 8 to see the boys
ie. Gwatkin Stopford +Geoffrey to try + get together
a statement. I haven't seen it but they went on
till after 1 in morning, much beer drunk
+ much smoking but Mr Gwatkin assured
me that W had been successful in getting a
better atmosphere.
This morning Friday 5th the foreign minister
+ Prime Minister returned the call all dressed
up again + at 1 we went off alone to lunch
with the President + Mme Benes. The old palace
is beautiful_ a succession of lovely rooms. We
wished we could have transplanted one to
London for our music room! + the taste is
simple, quiet + good. We had an excellent

Friday 5th
well served lunch just the 4 of us + after we moved
into another set of reception rooms - some
beautiful tapestries, few pictures. Mme + I talked
apart while W + Benes had a long talk. W
however came away a little dissatisfied
he got nothing definite out of B, + was afraid
to ask a definite question as to what he
would be prepared to do now at once by way
of concessions as regards apptments in post
office etc to Germans, in case the flow would
stop + he wd not ever get what Bwas then
ready to talk about. Mainly abt the political
position in general. W gathers that B cd put
through anything he wanted. The President can
preside over Cabinet when he likes as a rule
when the P. M asks him to, he also has a
veto on apptment of Cab: ministers besides of
course selecting the P. M. So as a rule in im-
portant offices he is consulted beforehand + he
is supposed to have special concern with defence
+ foreign affairs so apparently choses his
own ministers for these 2 departments. He is
a little man, not particularly prepossessing
but he was extremely cordial. I got on well
with Madame, but my French is quite atrocious
He speaks English, slowly but sufficiently.

we left at 3.15 + came straight back. We
now have the offer of the use of a Castle
only 16 minutes away with swimming pool
+ tennis court + shooting, but no servants
supplied. When I told W it was as from
1st Sept. he said we'd be hoofed out before
then, but that I do not believe!
Geoffrey wanted to have Mrs Peto very naturally
so she arrives today, perhaps only for a few
days returning again in September when
she is freer.
It is still very hot, but we both slept better las
night. We hope to dine at a cool high up restaur
ant this evening with view of River Moldava.
Saturday 6th.
We went out to this high cool place, the Hendersons Petos
+ us. Mr Henderson was at Innsbrück as Consul for some
years + all through the Anschluss. Mrs came + talked to
me one morning when they were still staying here + told me
pitiful tales of their friends - husbands sympathetic to
Habsburgs tho' not active sent off no one knows where
+ wives left behind penniless. She said the German troops
did preserve order + prevent bloodshed.
In the morning I had my German lesson. She is quite
intelligent I think + particular about my pronunciation

which is good.
We lunched at the Legation to meet some of the
other Foreign Ministers. U.S.A French Swiss . -
I sat between the 2 last. The Frenchman just
polite in bad English the Swiss who has been 11 years
here quite ready to talk - He thinks Benes the man of
brains - +that he ought to take up this affair
himself He also seemed to think he cd do what he
liked his position being strong enough. He also took the
view of many like him, that if France + England
together make it clear they will have no nonsense
Hitler will hesitate. His wife is a sister of Roose-
veldt's Minister of agriculture Mr Wallace. They were
both insignificant looking but I daresay both
very intelligent. I then had to talk to Mr Hugh Wilson
U.S. A Ambassador in Berlin, making a short
tour here + in Poland - I found him quite
stupid. He told me that the German Gov: paid
all salaries of Protestant clergy (not RCs) "as
you did", he cheerfully remarked, "till 50 years ago when
you disestablished the Church". I gaped + said
meekly one church was still established +
endowed but was not included in Budget!
He reluctantly took my view! He then talked
of Hitler with great admiration. Said if he were
German he wd be a disciple for what he had done

for his people to whom he was genuinely devoted
And no other human ties - I caustically remarked
he had made them into a cruel people - he said
truly, "he has done more than that," + that
you could be a disciple without agreeing with
everything your master did. ie. he might
not agree with all President R did + yet could
serve him. I nearly remarked that I thought
Ambassadors were not political. I thought it
improper of him to suggest to me that he had
any anti R' policy views. Then he gave
an example of Hitler's profundity of thought
Hitler had said + had obviously deeply impressed
him thereby, that you could not have a democracy
in a country which only produced 80% of its food
supply. This remark he invited me to agree
"made me think". I then cheerfully remarked
that we had somehow managed it + we hadn't
nearly 80% of our food home grown. He said we had our
Colonies to provide us with everything. I told him till
a few years ago we had no trading advantages
with them, then he said the £1 sterling was
the same all over the Empire so we had no
exchange difficulties - I gave it up then but I thought he
was wrong + so I gather now he was. But what a
foolish fellow, the result I suppose of the 'spoils system !

We stayed sometime talking in the pleasant Legation Garden
and only started rather late for Zdar where we
were to spend the weekend with Count + Countess Kinsky
a Czech nobleman. It was a good 2 hours motor
The Count + some young men had come out to meet
us at where the main road joins an estate
road - He thought we might like a little walk
in the forest before dinner. We just went a
little turn saw his beautiful big lake +
then got back into the car + drove to
the Schloss (Zámek in Czech) where we were
shown straight to our rooms all in suite
Hunter at the end. W's room opened off mine
but the others had separate exits into a passage.
The rooms were large + bare very wide planks
polished + a very occasional rug. No H+C
+ we only discovered one bath room with a geyser.
The air was delicious so fresh + cool, but the Castle
stands high I think over 1000 ft + the woods are
higher still. We weren't given long to dress + b[-]
we went along the passage to a vast domed
empty hall formerly the monks refectory (for the
Schloss was at one time a monastery). The high ceiling
had frescoes + it was an imposing place. There we
found some young men + Countess Princess Hohenlohe
( her husband arrived next morning.) She was the

Weekend at Zdar.
only other lady bar our hostess who is very tall +
slim with only a rare white hair tho' she is
said to be rather older than her husband. She
was previously Princess Schwarzenberg, also Czech
nobility, her second son was there. I found her
a little difficult to talk to + Mrs Peto I think
found the same. Princess Hohenlohe was very
sympathetic I enjoyed talking to her I think
she is a much cleverer woman. They are
Viennese + her poor husband seems nearly distracted
with all the new German rules + regulations +
interferences. What he minded most was having to
dismiss his Jewish employes. He is in business.
After dinner the first night we just talked
sitting round a big round table in front of the
sofa in usual German style.
On Sunday our host had made very definite
plans. In the morning to see round house
chapel (a vast Baroque [--] peu sur chargé dedans)
+ garden Then lunch at 12.30 then a roe buck
stalk for W + Mr Peto + I think one or two others
starting at 3.30.
Our Minister had kindly lent W his rifle which
however didn't fit very well. We started off with
6 car fulls for the forest. At our first stop we found
5 ponies in case, W wd like to ride over a forest

Aug: 6 - 8
path instead of driving by car which he did. I did
wish I could have gone too. We all met again at
a wooden hut with a lovely view so high it was
almost cold. When after waiting 20 minutes or
so the ponies + riders turned up we again
got into the car + drove to the lake where
we had been the first evening also where there
is a wooden hut. We dropped the sportsmen
en route. The rest of the males disported
themselves in the water + when the ponies
arrived they were made also to bathe. It was
gay + pleasant, but I wd. have liked a walk!
I managed a stroll later on! Princess Hohenlohe
didn't come, she had had a dog bite separating
a fight before coming to Zdar at her daughter's
house near. Finally the sportsmen arrived. W
had 2 shots but missed both. The keeper carries
a little trumpet on which he makes a noise
like the call of the doe + the poor little
bucks run forward to meet their loves, only
to receive their death - But none did
that afternoon. We spent hours in the forest
+ only got back in time for dinner - we persuaded
our hostess to play for us. She only played light
Viennese airs but with a good + strong touch
quite pleasant. I talked mostly to her 2nd son

The Mission Monday 8 - Monday 15th
a most excellent young man who is Dr of Laws +
is to be taken into the F.O I think next year.
NO nobleman I gather is yet a member of the
gov: but it seems entirely a good thing that
they should take some share in official life.
He expounded the history of his country.
We left early on Monday morning again by car
Count Kinsky came in ours as we wished
us to go past his castle Chlumec NC. The
other was really his wifes. He wanted to show
us the rooms which he hoped we would use
tho' they are not now in residence, any night
when we found Prague too hot. A really delightful
invitation. The Castle was built for the coronation
of Charles VI in Prague as the family decided
that the dungeons of the old Castle smelt too
badly. This was built in 6 mos. 1400 workmen
working day + night. Imposing baroque
huge central hall + central drawingroom
above, but really huge, the sitting rooms
open off the hall the bedrooms off the higher
room. These bedrooms have bathrooms etc all
complete. NO carpets though it must be very
cold in winter, but lovely polished wide boards
+ a very rare rug. The chandelier in round room
is magnificent, + there are lots of ancestral

pictures, + many pictures of horses as indeed
is the case at Zdar. I have never seen so
many prancing + gallopping steeds.
Our host is a cavalry office + devoted to horses. For the
last 100 years they have all the horses' pedigrees
complete, Before that day 2 or 3 hundred years
before they were a little mixed! One beautiful
cream stallion was shown to us, we had to
make a very brief visit to the stables which were
magnificent all done in our best "Sunday only"
style!
We only stopped a short while as W had to go on
to get back, but we were quite ready to accept
the invitation.
Monday.
We really only got back in time for lunch.
In the afternoon Dr Czerny (formerly of Czech legation
in London now here in F.O. + attached to the
Mission for introductions etc etc.) took Mrs Peto
+ me to see a glass exhibition a wonderful collection
but so hot we nearly expired. We also previously
went to a glass shop + saw lots of attractive things
but very dear. Then we had to cry off as Mrs Peto
every now again remarked she felt she might pass out
any minute which was alarming.
I don't think W saw anyone special that

day + we dined quietly alone here in the Hotel.
Tuesday 9th
This morning the Sudetens came again with
a detailed list of their grievances, W said very
like the Irish stories in old days. But the real snag
was that they refused to meet the Gov: committe
appted to negotiate with them because it
included no member of Cabinet, the speaker
was on it + some back benchers. The objection
didn't seem altogether unreasonable, how far
cd a back bench committee commit the Gov?
W seemed rather depressed over this. The
one thing he is anxious for is to get the negotiations
started, + to get them on actual practical points.
In the afternoon Mrs Peto + I went out with
Prince Schwarzenberg the 2nd son of Countess Kinsky
in his open car to look round. We went +
looked at the magnificent F.O. an old palace
but which having been used as barracks required
a great deal of expensive doing up. Madame
Benes is credited with getting space cleared +
an attractive garden made by it. Opposite
the F.O is the Loreta Church, [--] one of the
usual Baroque Churches, with a curious little

chapel in the centre of the cloisters. The Church
itself makes one rather ill so "surcharge".
The treasury has a wonderful collection of precious
things, monstrances set with jewels one with
hundreds of diamonds most brilliant + other
gold + silver + a great deal of decoration with
the Czech garnets. Prince S gave us a regular
little history lesson as we stopped in a square
outside a church. Very interesting.
I found his step father very sore on the "Geschichte
Lüge" which characterized Bruce Lockharts book
on Czechs, + from which the Times is not
free. ie. 1) that Bohemia had never been a
State before. The Czechs Mazarak +Benes etc
made out that they had created a new
thing when really it was a revival. Franz
Josef it is true never was crowned in Prague
but he always promised to be crowned + thereby
recognized Bohemia as a separate state.
2) The fiction that all the Slav nobility was
Killed in the Battle of the White Mountain.
Lots of Czech nobles are still here, + tho' some
have German names they are nevertheless
of Czech nationality + have been for 100s of years!
Of course he admitted that Bohemia being no
longer a Kingdom, the nobility went to court in

Vienna + that was a mistake. The Emperor ought
to have sent an Archduke to reside in Prague!
Tuesday evening we set out rather late for
Chlumec the Kinsky castle. When we arrived
after dinner we found not only young Schwarzen
berg but also Count Kinsky so afraid lest
in his absence we should not have all we
wanted. The air was a delicious change from
Prague. I went to bed at once being some-
what upset by the heat, but W stayed up
+ talked to our hosts + found it all very
interesting, said the Count was not so unpolitical
as he said, but he belongs to no party.
W was kept by conference.

Wednesday.
W went at 11 + had a good + on the whole very
satisfactory talk with Benes. He promised to look into
the matter of the composition of the Gov: negotiating
committee, + also made some promises as to
putting into action without delay the promises
of fairer play for Germans in the matter of
Gov: appointments, in which I think, all
recognize that they have a legitimate
grievance.
He later saw Hodza with whom he dined, men
only. And came back full of praise of him.
He told me he had told Hodza that he was one
of the most broad minded men he knew + it
seems that Hodza has now consented to come
to the negotiating committee + take the chair.
So "mediation" seems already to have had
some results. W told me also that Hodza said
that the Mission had had a great moral
effect, which also was comforting.
I had young Stephen Verney (Baliol) to tea + Charlotte
Bonham Carter turned up for a few days. Edgar is doing
a cure in Czecho Slovakia Charlotte as gay as ever
Thursday.
Again the Sudetens + I gather things went
better. I don't hear much detail as W naturally

coming up tired from these conferences doesn't
want to go over all the ground again with
me! He asked to see Henlein + they seemed
nervous about this + hoped it could be arranged
for the meeting to take place out of Prague
they apparently feared a demonstration in
Prague! So it is expected that he will come
to Prince Kinskys where we go for the week
end some way to North of Prague.
We had talked of going to Marienbad this
week end, but it thought rather soon, it is
feared that too much might be made of
our visit by the Sudetenpartei so we go
for a week end visit to Prince Kinsky. He
called in the afternoon to make arrangements.
Very ageeable polished speaks English well,
He said he had only a shooting box quite small
but comfortable, + then he enumerated a long
list of guests who are to come to meet us + said
we could bring as many as we liked, so we
guess his idea of a 'small' house is not ours.
Bob Boothby who has been losing 11/2 stone at
M Carlsbad came to tea to air his views.
We had everyone in to tea, quite pleasant
Bob thinks economics are the most influential

factor in their unrest + wants an international
loan for relief works etc. I don't know that he
contributed anything much new. He didn't seem
to think that most s.qs wanted an Anschluss.
Today, Thursday we lunched at the Ministers
I sat next him + next an official of F.O formerly
at Berlin legation. He maintained, which I
doubt, that my German was better than his
English so I did my best. I like our Mr Newton
he is natural + very pleasant + ready to take
trouble in the right way. He asked several
of the more business people to meet us + I
talked German with great energy to 2 or 3
Ladies. One a Czech widow of iron works very rich
she wants to lend us her house close to Prague
to sleep in, she is not there but it is completely
staffed I aim to see it this afternoon. A
nother wife was the wife of the Manager of the
State lands + forests I gather a good sportswoman
she only spoke German but was most forth
coming. W got on quite well between the
iron works widow + a FO. wife - I liked my
F.O official. He talked of Hitler of his bad German
+ lack of Education + of the impossibility of teaching
a dictator who starts ill equipped tho' he says

his language has improved. Like many people
he regrets that the fact that Hitler defied
the opinion of his generals over the Rhineland
incursion, + was proved right- He may so easily
now think he always knows better. They all seem
to think that the Generals do not want a war.
This FO. man is going to arrange some fishing
for us which will be fun, but the season is very
nearly over.
Most surprisingly W's guns have turned up in
good time for the first partridge shoot on 17th.
which is being arranged. They are told to bring
500 cartridges! We think Leslie must have sent
them, tho' I didn't actually ask him to!
We went out on the invitation of the Petos to
dine at Bärendov, a pleasant open air
restaurant. I had a long talk with Col. Strong
our military attaché also for Yugoslavia. His
view is that the S. Gs do want to be Nazi - he
says he has seen a lot of them.
He thinks the Czechs perhaps a little too confident
They count on lots of Russian aeroplanes + apparently
disregard the awkwardness of their having to fly
over Poland. They realize France can do very
little. He would like the impression to be given that
England is very interested (I think this Mission lends

colour to that view) but agrees that 'bluff' is very
dangerous in foreign affairs. He told me that Hitler
in Mein Kampf does point out how foolish
the German psychology was ^ in 1914 in not realizing
that England once in a war wd never let go.
I found this rather reassuring. the fact
that Hitler does realize this. He Col Strong didn't doesnt seem
much impressed with the War Minister who is
a civilian. W hasnt met him yet nor the Finance
Minister.
When we lunched with the President at the
Castle he proudly talked of his balanced Budget
+ received my compliments on the prosperity
of his country, + then he talked about a
second Budget which apparently doesnt balance
at all which seemed rather to alter the
situation. Now W says the finances are really
in a bad way!
Col: Strong hoped that Mr Hugh Wilson USA. ambassador
from Berlin wd be useful so I told him my impression
+ also that he appeared to be very impressed by
Hitler, to which Col S. said "They all are! our
Ambassador in Berlin also"! which was un-
welcome news. He then said he had been very
indiscreet but it was so, + I assured him I
had countless secrets locked in my heart!

Friday
We both slept badly. W looks tired. We wonder if
our week end will be tiring or refreshing!
We now learn Henlein cant come but that Max
Hohenlohe whom we met in London (+ whom
Count Kinsky described to me as extreme) +
who seemed to us reasonable! will be there +
will arrange a secon another place for meeting.
Today W saw the Hungarians till lunch time
+ after de Zullo "came up + as usual
chattered volubly in a mixture of English
+ German quite ununderstandable! He invites
us to marvellous fishing + shooting but a
nights' journey away I don't think we can
manage it, unless possibly much later.
Now I am going off with Madame Havrankova
who is calling for me at 3.30 to take me to
see the house she wants to lend us.
Little Zullo seemed to me to talk dreadful nonsense about
Benes being a Communist + not agreeing with Hodza
+ that the Hungarian party held the balance +
cd. make them Benes do what they wanted by
Parl: vote. I imagne all piffle. Anyhow I asked
Mme Havrankova abt parties. Hodza is Agrarian
= R. Benes not being a landowner or in any way
agricultural, cd not be agrarian + so became

R wing Socialist which Mme H assured me made it
quite easy for him to work with Benes Hodza +
indeed the Socialist party under his influence
was getting very moderate.
We went to the house in a terrible thunderstorm
It is very pleasant not in the country but
with a nice garden quiet + I shld say wd
be very comfortable. I hope we do go there
but nothing very definite has been proposed.
I after went to tea at the Legation.
I cried off a proposal to go to the Baroque Exhibition
with Mrs Henderson + Charlotte Mrs H didn't want to
go because of the Krofta dinner at the F. O.
This was a very swell affair. (Rather a
shortage of wives as many are in the country
with their children) abt 40 at dinner +
2 or 3 hundred for music after. I sat between
the host the Foreign Minister + the Speaker
former P. M. Neither very interesting, I talked a
mixture of French + German - quite a good dinner
+ in a fine room. The building is indeed magnificent
said to have been built by a Count Czernin, to
spite the Emperor Chas VI by having a finer
palace at Prague than he! It after became
a barracks till Benes when Foreign Minister
restored it + now it has many most
lovely rooms - wide imposing corridors. The

concert was a quartet string + piano all
quite good. After was rather exhausting
We moved to a room with buffet - endless
people were introduced +I did get very hot
+ tired. NO one very exciting. A charming
young opera (Vienna) soprano who begged
us to come out to her house +she wd sing to
us. Which I hope she will do.
Everyone very cordial. No indication that
the general public at the party were anything
but delighted at the Mission's arrival.
We got home late.
Saturday 13th.
I had a good 2 hours of German this
morning, then I meant to go for a walk
as I have really not walked in Prague
since we came.
W saw the Sudeten Industrialists. Some he
thought very able. They werent too hopeless.
but think they have suffered from Czech Gov:
discrimination in favour of Czech concerns.
At lunch we had Lord Allen whom I had met
at tea at the Ministers on Friday, + Mr

Catchpole a good little Quaker with a funny accent
who has been doing very good work in getting
money to relieve distress in Sudeten (very) depressed
areas. He sent in a very good + sad report
a year ago which now we all read. The conditions
are very bad.
Lord Allen apparently has seen Benes + Hodza
+ I dont know who else but seems to have
got a very satisfactory impression of the value
of the Mission as he told W. which was cheering
Tho' I wouldnt too much trust Lord A's judgment
it is pleasant that he got that impression
from his talks. I presume he has some influence
in Lab: circles of sorts.
After lunch we started for Balzhütte in N
Bohemia in Sudeten area to stay with
Prince + Princess Kinsky - (a real Fürst only the
eldest son holds the title) Mr Peto + Mr
Gwatkin came too. 2 cars.
About 2 hours journey + we arrived after 5 o'clock
The house is 3 picturesque wooden chalets
literally draped with caper cailzies with
heads + feathers spread out like a fan behind
+ horns of all kinds. Each having the name
of the man who shot it. They shoot their
capers with a rifle sitting stalking them

Weekend with Prince Kinsky.
in the mating season when they make a
strange noise after their little call, + during
this strange noise they are blind + deaf
+ the stalker creeps close up within range.
But he must remain absolutely still
while the other notes are sung + only move
at the right time. The roebuck they also
shoot with rifles as at Count Kinskys.
We found the Clary's there. I had
talked to her at tea on Friday at Legation
but had not a chance of talking to him,
also there were Count + Countess Khuen
from Moravia very German. The Claris
live near + went home to dress for dinner
+ came again. the others stayed and Hunter
could at last have some talk as Countess K's
maid talked English
Our hostess was very nervous. She had got a fright alone
with her small children here in May when the
Czechs moved up their troops. She thought war
had broken out + panicked when she found
the roads blocked to Germany. The soldiers were
rough + rude - When at last she could go she
dashed to Dresden only to find everyone in
the streets in their Sunday best and all quiet
+ calm. She is partly Argentine (Martinez de Hoz)

- Monday 15th.
It was an easy pleasant party in the one big
living room, table at one end.
On Sunday it was clear that our arrival
had caused great excitement among the
Sudetens. They crowded to the gate of the
drive + clamoured for W who had to go
+ just say a word. One or two shouted in
English. They regard him as their Saviour.
It is very touching + rather overwhelming.
These Sudeten aristocrats are convinced that
Hitler is really for peace. I wish I felt as sure.
They obviously dislike the Czech government
+ one can well understand a certain feeling
of contempt. Certainly the Czechs show no real
breadth of view or comprehension as to how to
govern a country such as this. From the
beginning they have encouraged their people to
regard the country as entirely theirs to rule as they
liked in their own interest. It is ridiculous that
in Sudeten area all postmen etc should be
Czech. And it is bad that even after the negotiations
were begun in March they still kept sending
new Czech officials into the Sudeten area to increase
the Czech population there, preference being
given to those with large families ! so they say!!
I thought Prince Clary very well informed + really

rather a charmer with his dark eyes inherited
from his remote Italian ancestors. Prince Kinsky
on the contrary was rather bitter, he took an
entirely hopeless view of the Czech character.
We did nothing special just walked about +
talked _ On Monday we stopped at the Clary's
for lunch at their small place. More open
than the Kinsky's forest bound dwellings
I preferred the Clarys. They also had antlers
+ capers all over but not outside!
We got back in the evening + found letters. Alas
bad news from Oliver it is very sad for poor Kit
to be disappointed again. I think there had been
some uncertainty + perhaps it didn't come as
a great shock, but I do feel terribly sad for both
of them.

Tuesday + Wednesday were difficult +strenuous
days for W.
He went to Benes on Tuesday to press the point
that something practical should be done at once
as a beginning + to show readiness to act
in the right way. Benes agreed.
Then the Sudetens said they would not negotiate
any more.
W had succeeded in getting Hodza to agree
that the negotiating committee must be
more than one of backbenchers + he had
consented to take chair + he brought others
with him so a start was made.
Then the SDP said it was useless to go on
No bridge was possible between such entirely
different conceptions.
They turned up on Tuesday night at 8.30pm
+ at 12.30 am W came to my room + said
he had got them to promise to go on negotiating
He said he teased them + chaffed them filled them
with beer + ham sandwiches (for which I trust
the Gov: will pay) + finally they agreed.
Then he got from the Prime Minister a very
important letter definitely promising that
certain named posts should forthwith be

given to Sudetens in their own districts. Mr
Henderson assured W that they were quite
substantial concessions. And W felt he
was armed at any rate with something
to take to Hitler Henlein.
W. feels really sorry for Hodza. He is himself
a broad minded man a Slovakian + I gather
a man of education - But he has great
difficulty with his colleagues who are alas
very different.
However we felt that something really had
been achieved. The negotiations to go on +
some move in the right direction made by
Gov:
Thursday.
We set out 10.30. for Schloss Rothenhaus
where the meeting with Chicken was to take
place. (He says he might be shot if he came to
Prague!) This is the residence of Prince Max
von Hohenlohe whom we saw in London, a
friend of Maggie Greville's We arrived in good
time for lunch. W + I in our own car with our rapid
but on the whole very good driver. G Peto + Mr
Gwatkin behind in another car.
It is an enormous house built round a vast

courtyard + simply stuffed inshad inside with every
sort + style, type of furniture - many real
treasures. A great deal from Spain. Our hostess
is Spanish + on death of her mother seems to
have managed to get a great deal of her
valuable belongings out of the country. In the
house near Madrid much has been destroyed
the house having been occupied by soldiers, not
I think Reds. The tapestries are very fine.
Spanish + there are busts + paintings + lots
of carpets + endless china, some Hohenlohe of
course. Our hostess is extremely voluble talks
like Lady Cunard has 6 children is full of
energy. We found when we arrived Henlein, Frank
his deputy, not actually on negotiating committee,
Kundt the chief member of that committee. I had to
sit next Frank ^ at lunch a big featured thin man not a
very attractive expression, he is said to be mis
trusted, because he wants to supplant Henlein.
Kundt is pleasant, looks like what he is + was
a miner. Henlein also looks exactly what he was
a well made rather benign gymnast. No much
indication of intelligence. I had no chance to talk to
him. Prince H was rather optimistic at lunch,
so when abt 2 hours later W came to my room
where I had been sent to repose after an exhaustive
to

tour of house + gardens, I was disappointed to hear
that the interview had not been encouraging.
Chicken professed to despise the concessions, W said
they are only a beginning, you must begin somewhere
but no, he wd not take that view, but of course when W
then said shall I then say you don't want them
of course again he had to say NO. Of course he wanted
them. Then he began to talk of "other means" +when
W said 'What are the other means except by
conference?' he wouldn't say, + finally had to agree
conference was the only way. So the meetings are
to continue!
However at the end, after tea, at which we all
assembled again as we were going he made
a polite little speech saying how grateful they
were to W, to which W suitably replied.
Then there was an excitement because a deputation
came from a neighbouring village saying that
owing to the election of a new (German) burgomeister
the Communists had been rioting for 3 days + the
police stood by + did nothing. So Gwatkin + Geoffrey P
decided to go + see. a message was sent to
Prague head quarters + some one was to be sent
down. They didn't find anything very terrible, tho'
a few Germans had been set upon + the police
tho' 150! were not enough to keep the crowds

in order, but Kundt disappointed them he was so un-
balanced + excited over the affair + they fear that
he was responsible for a very exaggerated version
which reached the Press (not local for that was
censored) However I think that was put right.
And W having asked for someone to be sent
from Headquarters, sent Mr Gwatkin's report
to P. M which pleased him naturally.
So one sees first hand an instance of
the difficulties which are added to this already
difficult problem, through the excitability +
unreliability of the aggrieved.
But the Germans have very substantial
grievances + it must be admitted (tho I
doubt if the Czechs even will,) that 20 years
of Gov: have proved them incapable of dealing
with this difficult country.
W had told me that Mr Kundt had wished to pay
his respects to me so I said how pleased
I wd be. I fear not knowing I addressed myself
too same Frank too, they were together + I didn't
know which was which. This was a mistake.
They said they'd come at 12 next day
Friday
So having secured the assistance of Mrs
Henderson who having been 6 years wife of

consul at Innsbrück cd speak German with ease. We
awaited the arrival. I had expected 2 or 3, but
a lovely basket of roses with 6 names make me
vaguely uneasy I asked for more glasses. It
was decided that they must be regaled with
sherry, but before we could get more chairs
or more sherry a whole unending stream
arrived 8 of them. Miss Miller hurriedly
produced chairs + after a time more sherry
+ glasses arrived.
I can get on pretty well now in German when
talking to one person. I can stop them + make
them repeat a word, but when 2 or 3 of these
good gentleman all talked to me at once
I was hopelessly stuck + found Mrs H a godsend!
We chaffed them + were very merry. I spotted
the one W calls Lord Essenden and found he was
only too delighted to be called after so rich +
distinguished a man. They asked if W was a
"composer" they I said no but he was very fond
of music + I wd suggest if ever they found him
very difficult they should at once sing some
thing very beautifully + he would yield at
once. This they found very funny (mercifully!!)
As also when I said they ought some day to go to
England, they said perhaps we wd invite them

I said if you are all very good we will, they said
Aren't we all very good. I replied I did not know!
And so we went on. I thought it most necessary
to keep off anything serious + apparently we
did. Anyhow they stayed an hour + a most
strenuous hour I found it! I dared not offer a
second glass of sherry in case they never went!
Thursday evening.
We had rather a rush returning from the
Hohenlohe's to get to the Legation tho' dinner was
8.30. It was rather a dull party, only 4 women
including Princess Hohenlohe + myself. The Hohenlohes
were asked because we were to have stayed the
night there + only at the last moment learnt of
this dinner! Also W was never told it was black tie,
how badly they do their job!
I sat between a Count Ledebur formerly a
Senator +now I gather rather pro S D. P. +
the Roumanian Minister who was bright +
easy to talk to in French. Ledebur spoke
English. The Roumanian told me they were
getting something done to satisfy their minorities
I hope they'll succeed. They ought to have done it long
ago! He spoke of old Masaryk as a broad minded
man, but said tho' he sympathised with Minorities
he didn't like Minorities of the Right! + I daresay

that is the reason he did nothing^ much for the Sudetens.
After dinner I talked to wife of Czech ex consul at
Dublin. They seemed to have quite sound views
on Irish politics! Then I talked to wife of German
Chargé. They had not very long returned from
9 years in Russia - thankful to leave. She was
quite pleasant I had to talk German to her.
We got home very late.
The negotiations go on + that is about all
that can be said, I suppose presently the
2 sets of proposals can be laid side by side
+ it can be seen what accommodation can be
got. It seems to me that the Czechs must go
a very long way towards Home Rule for internal
affairs. They don't seem to realize what a mess
of it they have made when after 20 years
of ruling, they have made nearly 1/2 their
population entirely discontented.
Friday - evening we didn't do anything much
We had both Hendersons to lunch which was
pleasant.

Saturday 20 - 21st Weekend in S. Bohemia
We started at abt 10.45 in 2 cars Young Prince
Franzi Schwarzenberg taking Geoffrey P + W + I in ours
for Oberplan to be guests of another Schwarzen
berg Prince Adolph, (Fürst on death of his father
now ill in Wien) W was upset to learn how far
we had to go + it was a very hot + exhausting
day. We broke the journey at Prince Carl's
place or rather I think his mother's wife's place
She wasn't there we were rather amused by his
comic cynicism. Franzi took us, the brothers seem
to be on good terms. F is in Gov service Home
office + later he is to enter the F. O. Mr Peto says he
is very pro Czech.
We got to a town I forget its name where we were
met by Prince Adolph's head manager Mr Nikaulay
He was a great fellow. There was a little crowd waiting
outside the hotel + some other Foresters or
Huntsmen (they seem to combine both functions)
belonging to the Prince's estate near by. Here he has
a house modelled on Windsor Castle, we saw its
vast tower in the distance - We descended + I
had to be polite in German + then the head man
got into our car to conduct us personally the
remaining miles 40 or 50 I shd say. He was
most informing about everything + I understood fairly

tho' in his enthusiasm for the object to be admired
he sometimes gazed at it instead of at me!
which made it hard to hear.
The scenery was lovely. Everywhere we seem
to see splendid crops + in these remoter parts
we often saw quite a pretty village with steep
sloping dark red roofs - The hills + mountains
are everywhere covered with trees.
Eventually we arrived at a little wooden
house. Standing outside was a little crowd of
villagers to receive us +as the we drove up
they shouted "Heil" + raised their arms. They
stayed some time + if I looked out of the
window at once a further chorus of Heil
arose, so they watched us quite closely
until we went out again after tea!
At the door our host greeted us, a short fat
little man with rough hair round head turned
up nose + little eyes. Not one's idea of a
Fürst! He at once told us that he lived some
miles away + hoped we would lunch with
him next day on our way home, he then showed
us our bedrooms + bathroom + salon said we
must have some tea +then his Manager wd
look after us + see what we wanted to do, fish
or shoot etc. He also said his [---] personal man servant

would took after us. Which indeed he did he unpacked
all my things + set them out most punctiliously!
Mr Peto had stopped with Franzi to see an enormous
castle belonging to Adolph now only a museum
he never lives there + no one has for ages. So W + I
were alone. After tea we set out to fish. We in a
light little phaeton drawn by a pair of grays with
one Jäger in box beside the Kutscher who wore
a livery + billycock. There other Jäger including
our Herr Nikaulay followed in another phaeton
with brown ponies. W tried fishing but lost the
only one he actually hooked. They don't fly fish
much, they prefer a worm or a grasshopper !!
So then we went off to the forest to try +get a
roe buck. We got out of the carriage + in the
rapidly increasing gloaming crept over the
rough ground to the edge of the forest. We saw a
buck but none came near enough for a shot.
But the stillness + evening light was so beautiful
we loved the whole thing. It was after 8 when we got back
We found Geoffrey P reading a book + full of the
wonders of the castle. We had dinner the
servant bringing up one intoxicant after
another in hope of persuading the Lord to drink!
Then we had a sweet fresh air to sleep in
after a short thunderstorm - Next day

Weekend in Oberplan S. Bohemia.
we spent all morning driving in the forest on
grassy paths going very quietly. then stopping
getting out trying for a roebuck then on again
Sometimes the road was very stony + very near
a precipice + very narrow, but the horses were
perfectly behaved. We liked it all enormously
There is nothing at home like these vast
forests. The wood is beautifully cut + piled
+ measured along the road whence it is fetched
by the purchaser - It is a real business + the woods
are very well kept. The trees live often 4 or [5]
hundred years, recently they felled one of
600 years. +.
We got back in time to change to our car,
so again accompanied by Mr Nikaulay for the
50 minutes run to Prince Adolph's other
house for lunch. This seemed even smaller
than ours. Only 1 sitting room 2 bedrooms + bathroom.
We were well waited on + fed except that poor W could
not bear the very sour rye bread, no white was
given us. The Princess is from Luxembourg
They have no children + lead a most restless
life going from one little house to another,
+ every now + then off to a farm in Kenya. I
felt that the Princess wd have liked a slightly more
stable existence. She too is a sportswoman + has shot

her 3 lions! They were very pleasant - We left at 3
for our 3 hours motor home again, This time the
journey was bearable it was quite cool + raining.
Meantime our 2 staff + the Hendersons had been
to a fair in Sudeten territory where they got far too
much of an ovation. We didn't dare risk going our-
selves. Mr Gwatkin even had to make a short
speech!
Our weekends are difficult to arrange. Invitations
are so numerous + a certain balance has to be
preserved between Cs + SDPs.
It seems a Czech industrialist wants us this
next Sat: but we have stuck to our plan of going
to Prince Clary's at his big schloss not the little
house where we lunched on our return from
Prince Kinsky's.
Monday 22.
Last night Mr Gwatkin told us that he was
invited to Marienbad to lunch with Max to
meet Chicken again. He was much excited
over this.
After the last interview on Thursday Max told W
that Chicken was embarrassed by a new offer from
Benes which they hadn't had time to consider

Mission to Prague
Benes had not communicated this new proposal
to the Mission which he might have done.
When W + I sat down to discuss G. P. came to say that
Gwatkin^ had got back + so off W went. Away from his dis-
approving eye I ordered schrimp soup, but they brought
me real turtle instead I guess out of a tin but very "good".
G's report was favourable. Chicken was ready to
negotiate on B's new plan. The only doubt was if it
really was B's as it had been given them by a
German Professor in the university.
W so excited he cd hardly sleep. Everyone hopeful.
23 Tuesday
W went + saw President. Came back reassured
Hodza came out as he went in, beaming.
(There had been so rumours that H had had his
own plan + was going to resign!! but apparently
all illfounded). The plan had full approval
of Benes, so if accepted by Henlein it really
looked as if progress cd now be made.
In afternoon however Kundt came for a long
interview with W + Gwatkin the latter interpreting +
K was very obstinate showed no inclination towards
any compromise whatever + W correspondingly
became depressed again!

August 22 - 29 .
W [----] However it later transpired that Kundt had had
quite a satisfactory talk with the President
who sent a special message to W next
morning to tell him things were going well.
Mr Hodza came to dine alone with us on
Wed: Tues. : evening. He looked to me a very tired man
+ indeed he did not make light of his difficulties
with 6 heads of 6 different parties to carry
with him in the unwelcome (to them) task
of concessions. I liked him, he was formerly
connected with Ferdinand + tho' he had some
severe criticisms to make on F's haughty
character when I asked him he said he
thought if he had lived he might have managed
to save Austria through his liberal policy. Mr Hodza
had a great feeling for Vienna + regretted deeply the
loss of that special Viennese culture not by any
means wholly German which had its own special
characteristics - He said first rate opera + theatre
second only to the Arts Theatre of Moscow.
As he left he said very nice things of W, + how
glad he was to have him. He also spoke of W's
great popularity all through Czslovakia.
At lunch time we had the 2 Schwarzen
berg brothers. Carl amuses me a great deal
Franzi is very pleasant + clever but not

of the same humorous wit.
I talked to Mr Gwatkin in the evening he also dined
with us + I found him very hopeful about
everything - said even if Kundt was
obstinate if Chicken agreed K wd have to
follow suit.
In afternoon Mrs Strong + I took Hunter for some sight seeing.
Wednesday.
Kundt had a long talk with President today.
Our young men went to a S. D. Club in Prague
that evening + drank much beer + brandy,
but learned that things were going well.
It poured so hard all day we never went
out at all -
Margie telephoned to Miss Miller who was out
but never asked for me + gave no clue as to
where she was. I got a letter however from
D. F. I think next day. saying she was coming + letting me know
he was perhaps sending money c/o me. So I rang
up Ambassadors Hotel but heard she hadnt arrived.
Thursday. 25 August.
Rang up + found she not yet arrived - but in
afternoon a police message came that she had arrived
in Prague aerodrome + we soon got into touch + she
came along here to tea. Afraid we would be annoyed

at the most unexpected publicity she had received. She
never dreamt she cd be discovered. She stopped first
at Frankfurt ? or Cologne + was told to go via Nuremberg
owing to weather, then reached Pilsen but had to
stay the night owing to rain - But at Pilsen
she was received with photographers, flowers +
fruit in her room + when she started next
day (after having been shown round the Brauerei
the famous sight naturally in Pilsen) she was
given a military escort which as it went
twice as quick as her little plane had to make
circles round her to keep in touch.
This evening was Madame Havrankova's musical party
we asked + took her with us where she had a great
success flying ladies being rare in C/Svia. And of
course they all thought she was only about 18!
Music very nice + everyone as usual very friendly.
We were given supper at 2 tables in a room sitting
down with selected guests while the general company
had only a buffet! We stayed the night, not very
comfortably - The noise of trams was great +
the floppy duvet + one thin blanket buttoned into
an untuckable sheet was very unmange
unmanageable -
Mr. Gwatkin had left on Wed: for London on
private business + also to see FO. N. Henderson

at Berlin not up to it, he seems hysterical + very
ununderstanding, urges that W shd make a
pronouncement I imagine a pro S D P one to
appease the Führer - While W's great point is
that he is not going to pronounce judgement which
indeed wd be a very silly + indeed fatal thing to do
His task is get the 2 sides to agree, a very different
matter but the only possible way to reach a peaceful
settlement.
Just as we were starting for the party Mr Stopford
came up to say telegrams etc had come in
which Gwatkin thought might modify our week
end plans. G. in London was to suggest some reliable
fellow to go to Berlin + keep N. H right especially
in view of Fuhrer's Nuremberg speech which it is
very important shd not be disastrous! Whether
anyone or anything can influence H, is hard to
say. However Stopford jumped to the conclusion
+ rightly that they ie. FO wd want W to go to
Berlin - He was quite sure that wouldnt do for
various reasons It wd alter his position here as an
independent mediator + if he failed + after his
visit H still made a provocative speech his
position here wd be ruined + his work undone.
So he definitely said NO at once.
He went + had a long consultation with the Minister

Friday. 26 (Lell's birthday)
Mr Troutbeck 1st sec came to see him this morning
so far I have heard nothing.
But Frank is making mischief. He has apparently
produced a memorandum which was censored here
but came on German wireless. We believe F is
out to make trouble + to supersede Chicken!
This manifesto said time to come for Germans to defend
themselves which sounded bad then it later said
legal advice wd be taken as to how this should be
done which made it sound quite mild, but
the English press seemed to get very excited abt it.
Pressure continues to make W go to Berlin but
he won't. If Hitler invited him it wd be another matter:
In the evening we went to National Theater. At
lunch we met a widow Schwarzenberg who lives
in Prague, very attractive bright creature +her
brother Count Schönborn a seedy looking creature but
quite pleasant + he secured a box for us. Being
"natural" it seems any number of officials have
a box so it was easy enough. We enjoyed the
performance greatly - It was Czech music +
they do seem to understand it Smetana I
am told didn't like it being so very much
performed as he regarded it as operette only

Die Verkaufte Braut, but the dance orchestra etc all
very good, + the light gay music was refreshing.
Saturday. 27th
We were to have gone to Prince Clary for lunch,
in time for a partridge shoot but cd not get away
till late, just in time for dinner - W had interviews
+ had to wait to see Gwatkin on his return from
London. G apparently approved of idea of W going to see
H. but W quite unmoved.
It seems a pity that we haven't now in Berlin a
better man than N Henderson. Margie had
heard a very poor account of him when she + R
were in S America, true many years ago but
still! He seems unbalanced.
We finally reached Teplitz abt 7.30 Found crowds of
S.D in space in front of the castle + were
greeted with much cheering. These poor people
had been standing for hours! + remained standing
long after we arrived I suppose hoping for a
glimpse of us! Peto + Gwatkin both came but
Peto G left after dinner with Prince Max for Rothenhaus in
order to see Henlein - There were 18 at dinner.
The Max Hohenlohes, the Ct. Ledebur + Countess
de la Tour a married (Belgian) sister of Prince Clary,
+ an old Tante, Schwarzenberg I think a widow

who lives in Berlin, 3 sons + a daughter + I think an
odd young man Kinsky. It is a large schloss,
successive buildings have been destroyed one
after another in the constant wars of this
country, but it is full of historical association
a bust of Napoleon stands in front of the General
Schwarzenberg who defeated him at Leipzig.
Recently they came upon some 200 pictures
hidden away from the time of Marie Teresa
they had records of these but believed they had
perished, so many have by dirt + damp but
some are restoreable, mostly family portraits.
After dinner W had to see the burgomeister etc.
+ I talked mostly to the Viennese Tante + Ctesse
Ledebur who seems to me to be nearly mad
she is so excited. When I mentioned that Franzi
Schwarzenberg (Czech in politics) had been so useful
as a guide because his knowledge of history was
so good, she nearly screamed at me that it
made her miserable that I shd let him talk
history to me, "he will tell you all wrong" she moaned
"I cannot bear it". I tried to pacify by telling her
I didn't talk politics to Franzi, but the history
of Baroque art + architecture + dates of pictures etc.
This just illustrates how excited + unreasonable they
are. They are just quivering! But Ctesse Ledebur
especially so!

: Teplitz
The most interesting guest was Clary's sister Mme de la Tour.
She is clever + nice. She has a wonderful album of
signatures, not autographs she says because they
are only of people she knows. Lots of royalties, a
boxer, a dancer, a film star, 2 dictators,
politicians, etc. nearly everyone. Hitler was sent
the book + asked for a signature + separately a
photo. He sent a signed photo + the book was
returned to him pointing out that he had not read the
instructions. He obeyed all right next time!
She spoke to me of Hitler ^ whom she meets sometimes says she doesn't think he
will live very long! She asked him what wd happen
if he died tomorrow: He said it will continue for a
short time. He told her that for the time being Nazism
was the one necessary gov: for Germany, but he
said it wd par exemple be no good in England with
her monarchy + democracy she has the Government
she wants (needs!) She also is convinced H doesn't want war
he said to her why shd I wish to destroy what I have am trying worked
so hard to build up! But that doesn't prevent his
war mongering propaganda. She said she didn't like
Hitler.
The old lady from Wien with a little frizz in front +
hair on top of her head was pathetic. She doesn't think
she can bear to go on living in Wien now. Her son of course
has "the estates + she a flat in Wien. For the first time she

Rothenhaus. 28 Aug:
wishes she had been born English :
W + I had large not realy very comfy rooms looking on to
the streets with windows opposite rather uncomfortably
near! + Prince Clary told me that they had to be careful [--]
in their Partridge shoots not to shoot into the houses.
On Sunday we set off in cars till out of the
town + then walked in the woods - Two detectives
ahead of our little procession + two behind.
They now seem all keen on having an International
police force, they are terrified of incidents.
The Czech police are excited as well as the SD,
+ there are bodies of Communists ready to make trouble.
However W can't mix up this: with the big questions
he has to fight on.
We talked after lunch. - The local + recently elected
burgomeister + wife came to lunch bringing bouquets
for Margie + me + a soap magnate (Leverhulme's Co)
Then at 4 we set out for Rothenhaus to meet
Henlein etc. Margie + I felt rather de trop but the
young daughter + her friend took us round the garden
+ someone rescued Hunter from the car, Then
the Princess appeared noisy + friendly as usual
+ brought us in to tea which we had as before
at a large well spread table. Herr Kundt turned up
quite soon rather solemn, + later Chicken himself
who always looks quite serene with his

pleasant quite simple face. He was going
to see Hilter. W. thought this a much better plan than
that he should go.
Poor Kundt looked very weary. He confessed to having had
too little sleep. He had invited Mr Stopford out to see him that
week end. Mr S when he arrived wondered which room
there was for him in the little house with Mrs K + children
but he was in due course conducted to a schloss
inhabited by an old lady of 85 a feeble minded son
+ a companion who spoke English. The F-M son however
supplying the English word when no one else cd think
of it! No previous introduction was thought necessary +
Mr S dined + slept there a solitary guest quite happily.
There is something very attractive about
the Rothenhaus atmosphere. The Spanish Princess
is so hearty + kind, the children play happily
about + everyone seems at home there.
Henlein was very courteous but I had no real conversation
with him.
Margie enjoyed these 2 visits enormously.
Monday. 29th
Great fun having Margie. We went out sight seeing
with Franzi, + saw cathedral + the big halls + then I
left to meet (Mme Bagnory who didn't come) + M went
on. Franzi took her to tea with a Czech dame whom

M found very ordinary! but she tried to persuade M to
fly her to call on the Batas. which I thought rather
cool. However we managed to avoid this next morning
when both this lady + Madame Bata rang up. Young Bata
made such a violent pro Czech speech that W decided
he cd not be visited at any rate at present. And anyhow
his works are very far away a night journey by train.
In evening Geoffrey P took M out to dine with his
widow whom we had already met at lunch with
her brother the seedy looking Count Schoenborn +
M found that quite amusing. Meantime we had
our Minister + young Macdonald of Times. A
highland youth of pleasant looks + manners, who
has travelled a lot in Russia + Germany. Knows Stalin a
little + thinks his days are few + that is partly why
his purges have recently been so complete. He is so
afraid that his work may be undone by a return to
extreme Trotsky ism.
The Minister is very pleasant. He stayed some time
waiting for copies of new Benes proposals. Our poor
girls were at it hard with no pause for dinner
till well after 10 pm. The Minister + W read their copies
+ agreed that it was unsatisfactory more vague
promises. not precise enough. B is very reluctant
to commit himself to any sort of generous proposal.

August. Monday 29 - Sunday. 4th.
Tuesday 30th.
I think it was this day ^ no I think next day? we lunched with Geoffrey P
to meet the Colerado Mansfields. They are friends
of Clive Morrison-Bell whom we saw here once
or twice, their Schloss is near Prague. The wife
is French. We were to have dined with them one
night but an approaching family demise put
us off. The Count is just a jolly old sporting squire,
she is French not very attractive I thought Margie
managed to talk with her.
On Tuesday afternoon M + went off to an S.D tea
party at Madame Bagnory. This was arranged by
Count Westphalen her brother. It was very
pleasant but the weather was appalling
violent thunder. M had gone off sightseeing
with a goggle eyed 1/2 Jap gent she had met
with Countess Kinsky's (Geoffrey's widow) + had a
real break down, car stopped, water in engine,
+ all available taxis seemed in same
plight so eventually goggle eyes stopped a
private car in which sat a lady + she
kindly brought M back while he rushed home
to change his drenched clothes. As it happened
the lady was the wife of the social editor of the
TagsBlatt so M's adventure filled its columns
next day!

The party was well done I struggled hard to speak
German with various good ladies; who are mostly
interested in relief work + kinder sorgen in
depressed SD areas. I met with Mrs Kundt a very
nice woman trained as a sick nurse she told me,
+ Mrs Frank not so attractive but all very pleasant.
M found some French speakers + had an easier time
Clarys + Ledeburs were also there but I devoted
myself to the others .
When I got back I found 2 presents from Herr
Frank, a hand made lace cloth which has
taken 540 hours to produce. Good design +
a rather ugly goblet, both of SD. local industries.
One day this I think Tuesday week we had the French Minister to
lunch, quite pleasant nothing remarkable. His
wife is away expecting the next first grandchild .
He told us his house was next the Bagnorys'. really
part of it. I didn't gather that they minded
having the smaller house, but I think they wd
glady have kept their nice garden - Another
instance of Czech "land reform"!
This was the night we would have dined + slept
with the Colerado Mansfields.
I think W went + saw President one of those days

+ talked very frankly to him. But he is not very
pliable.
Wednesday 31
Madame Havrankova came + took us
out M + me to a tea party where we met
many Czechs. I guess another "land reform"
estate in which a modern bungalow is
built with a very well laid out garden
very pleasant summer residence. We had a
very nicely served tea + much conversation.
I talked mainly to the Professor of History of Art
a friend of Sir Eric Macfadyen he says he
arranged the Baroque Exhibition + is coming to
London next year for some vast Art Exhibition.
History of Art I gather. The host made a pretty little
speech abt gratitude to W + wishing success etc.
which I value more coming from a Czech.
Thursday 1st.
We were all invited to dinner at Madame Kralish
Randa - rich industrialists where I had previously
been invited to play bridge. I sat between my
host + the [ ] , I found the host
quite interesting, he travels a great deal + spoke
French quite well (not English) + had a good deal

to say about Germany. The Italians he says just mock at
the idea of friendship with Germany. He said there
was shortage in G. but he thought no undernourishment.
The children looked well + healthy. But he said if you
go out to dine your hostess may apologise for lack of
meat or butter which was that day unob-
tainable. but there was enough. Only he said not
for a war! He thinks Hitler wants to avoid war,
but like everyone else feels him to be incalculable -
When a man regards himself and is regarded as
un Dieu, one can never foretell what he may do.
Mr Kralish Randa has a fine collection of old books,
we were invited to lunch one day to see them.
After dinner the young pianist who played for to us
at the F. O. party played again very agreeably.
We left early leaving Margie behind but she
found an escort.
Thursday. 2nd
We took M with us to lunch at Legation. I
sat next the Chancelier of the President. ie. the
head of his department, but the Minister didn't doesnt seem
to think he really counts for very much. He was
a real typical complacent Czech. He even
invited admiration for their having left in
the palace portraits of Marie Theresa, I

could only say 'Pourquois Ppas' + the old Abbé
on my other side weighed in with severe
condemnation of the destruction of a
fine statue of Marie Teresa in some
Czech town. I didn't like my partner.
But the old Abbé was charming in his
white Carmelite robes + lovely emerald +
diamond cross. He spoke French, badly
the Czechs have a horrible accent, but delighted
me by confessing a great enjoyment of detective
stories, Philip Oppenheim + Agatha Christie.
He wont speak English but he can read it.
Thursday night.
G. Peto Gwatkin W + I went off to dine
with Mr Preiss. We had hoped to stay night
but F said he must get back.
We found the Preiss wooden houses in most
beautiful country, very fresh indeed cold
air - The old man is a great fellow, head of
the biggest Bank + their leading industrialist
now. They had a good talk, outside + then in
the little secondary hut reserved for guests.
While Mrs + I chatted inside. I found her
a sensible woman no doubt reflecting her
husbands broad views, I quite enjoyed talking

to her. She told me details of her life. She had only
married Mr P 2 years ago because she feared to
worry him with her daughter, his own 3 by earlier
marriage all being married. However as Mrs P,
daughter wd. not make up her mind to marry. they
waited no longer but set the daughter up in an
establishment of her own + then married she had
divorced her husband years ago.
She told me that Mr P had long ,, ago urged on Benes that
he must do something, but he didn't not see it
in the same way. She also told me that Benes
was not a man of broad view tho clever.
She also said that in her husband's view what
Hitler really wanted with regard to Czechoslovakia
was not so much redress for S. Ds but to
secure the neutrality of C.Slvia. He dislikes their
French + Russian Alliance. Apparently the old
man also expressed this view to the men.
+ we are to dine again alone in a few days.
We got back abt 11.30 + found that Margie had
been out to the aerodrome as she had planned
taking young Clary with her to help her
to restrain enthusiastic wd-be helpers. She
found the aerodrome crowded with people
expecting the Lindbergs who failed to turn up

+ so had to fall back on photographing her!
She had everything in order + decided that
as the weather seemed so much better
she ought to go next morning. She had Ann
on her mind whom she had deposited at
Doxford + her husband.
Friday 2nd.
I got up at 7 + we went off to aerodrome
which we found quite deserted and after
the usual preliminaries customs passport
+ weather. M finally got off abt 8.30.
The little machine looked so tiny as it soared
off into the light clouds + disappeared.
She wired from Frankfurt which she reached
well before midday 11.30 I think + later we
had a wire telling of her safe arrival in
England. She wired that the weather was 'ideal'
so all was well.
As Margie was not available I asked Mrs Peto
if she wd come out to lunch at Mme^ Lowensteins.
There had been a muddle abt her invitation to shoot
so this was by way of a politesse to make up.
We had a drive of only about an hour tho'
uncertainty of road made it a little longer

Mme Lowenstein was most kind - She has a large
not very interesting house + gave us a very nice lunch
with just her daughter. Then she took us out in a
phaeton with 2 illmatched horses. I fear the rumour that
I enjoyed driving behind horses at Prince Adolph's has
gone round so this is now provided everywhere!
She evidently has a large estate farm land as well as
forest which since her husband's death she runs. He
seems to have been a very able head of Skoda
I think Jew: They had an extraordinary chandelier
made of stags horns, a rival to the Clary's arm chair
I wanted to get back not knowing what W was
doing.
The P had sent for him again - He apparently told
the French Minister he wd take Ws advice + he certainly
asks for it but I fear doesnt like it when he gets
it. W always comes back from these interviews saying
"unsatisfactory" when I enquire. After one interview I
think on Thursday, he confessed to feeling quite sorry
for him, he thinks he has trouble with his people.
And no wonder, it is his own fault. For 20
years he has taught the Czechs to think the country
was theirs + that in time they would Czechize the
Germans if they pursued a deliberate policy agst
them. + it is very hard to have to eat one's words in
such quantities! When W got back from P Kundt

was waiting, so I went on ahead to Legation with
clothes enough for one night. We had really
decided to see if W wouldnt sleep better up
in that nicer fresher air + really very pleasant
surroundings. We were only a party of 4. Mr Hodza
the P. M being the only guest. We began dinner
without W as he was so late but he soon came
in. We talked general semi historical conversation
till near the end. Then poor old Hodza showed how
anxious he was + he seemed to agree with all
they said ie that the time for reservations was past
something big must be done. Hodza thought the
S.D plans impracticable - the country is in
so many places just a strip, impossible to
administer separately. If it were a solid piece
it would be so much easier. W told Hodza that he had
been much impressed, during the interview he
had just come from, with the admirable way in
which Kundt had put his case. Hodza then
